Name: relational_geometry_probing
Title: Do Scientific Foundation Models Reconstruct the Periodic Table? Probing for Emergent Relational Ontologies in Representation Geometry
Short Hypothesis: Established science organizes entities into structured relational ontologies with known geometry: the periodic table (a 2D group/period lattice with periodicity), phylogenetic trees, reaction-class hierarchies, and functional-group taxonomies. We hypothesize that a foundation model which genuinely understands a domain will spontaneously embed these entities in a representation subspace whose geometry is *isomorphic* to the true relational structure (e.g., element embeddings recover group/period axes and chemical-family clusters), and that the fidelity of this recovered geometry is a read-only diagnostic that (a) distinguishes genuine structural understanding from co-occurrence memorization and (b) predicts the model's downstream generalization to held-out entities and relations.
Related Work: Recent work shows unsupervised low-dimensional manifolds of materials autonomously segregate superconductor families (Kim et al. 2026) and that scientific models globally converge in representation space (Edamadaka et al. 2025), but neither tests whether a *pretrained foundation model* recovers a specific, textbook relational ontology with its known geometry (axes, periodicity, tree metric). Word-embedding analogy work (king-man+woman) probed linear relational structure in general text, and 'emergent world models' work (Othello-GPT) showed board geometry recovery, but these target games/generic semantics, not established scientific taxonomies with quantitative structural ground truth. Interpretability studies of scientific models test whether categorical concepts (binding sites, motifs) are present, not whether the *relational geometry among many entities* is isomorphic to a known scientific ontology. Our contribution is a novel, read-only structural-isomorphism test: we measure how well a model's entity-embedding geometry matches a domain's canonical relational structure and link that fidelity to generalization. This differs from all my prior proposals (causal intervention, scaling exponents, cross-model universality, superseded-theory competition, conservation invariance), which target laws, exponents, cross-model agreement, historical errors, or symmetry rather than relational-ontology geometry.
Abstract: A hallmark of scientific understanding is placing entities into a structured relational order: elements into the periodic table's group/period lattice, organisms into phylogenetic trees, molecules into functional-group and reaction-class hierarchies. We ask whether foundation models for chemistry, biology, and materials spontaneously reconstruct these canonical ontologies in their representation geometry, and whether doing so signals genuine understanding versus co-occurrence memorization. We introduce Relational-Geometry Probing: for a domain with a known ontology, we extract embeddings of many entities, then quantify how isomorphic the embedding geometry is to the ground-truth relational structure. For the periodic table we test whether low-dimensional axes recover period and group, whether chemical families form separable clusters, and whether periodicity (repeating trends across periods) appears. For hierarchical ontologies (phylogenies, reaction classes) we measure how well embedding distances recover the tree/graph metric. We define a Relational-Fidelity Score combining axis-recovery R^2, cluster purity, and metric-correlation with the true structure. Crucially, we validate the score by testing whether high-fidelity geometry predicts generalization: models with more faithful geometry should better extrapolate properties to held-out entities and interpolate to synthetic/rare entities placed by structural position, whereas memorization-driven models should not. We apply this across open molecular (ChemBERTa/MolFormer), materials, and protein/sequence models of multiple sizes, comparing against randomly-initialized and co-occurrence-shuffled controls. The result is a cheap, reproducible audit of whether scientific foundation models encode the organizing structure of their fields, not just isolated facts.
Experiments: 1. Ontology curation (~10 relational structures across domains): chemistry — periodic table (group/period lattice + chemical-family labels), functional-group taxonomy, reaction-class hierarchy; biology — phylogenetic tree over a set of well-characterized proteins/organisms, Gene Ontology sub-hierarchy, amino-acid property lattice (hydrophobicity x size); materials — crystal space-group/Bravais-lattice hierarchy, composition-family structure. Each ontology provides ground-truth coordinates (lattice positions), cluster labels, or a tree/graph distance matrix. 2. Models: open molecular transformers (ChemBERTa, MolFormer), a public materials encoder, and ESM-2 at multiple sizes; extract per-entity embeddings (element tokens via minimal probe molecules, molecule/protein pooled embeddings, materials-composition embeddings). 3. Geometry recovery: (a) for lattice ontologies (periodic table, aa-property lattice), fit low-dimensional axes (PCA/PLS/canonical alignment) and measure R^2 of recovering period and group coordinates, plus detection of periodicity (repeating group-trend structure across periods via autocorrelation of a group-axis projection); (b) for cluster ontologies, measure cluster purity / silhouette against family labels; (c) for hierarchical ontologies, compute Spearman correlation between embedding pairwise distances and true tree/graph distances, and cophenetic correlation of embedding-derived vs ground-truth dendrograms. 4. Relational-Fidelity Score (RFS): aggregate axis-recovery R^2, cluster purity, and metric-correlation per ontology and layer. 5. Controls: randomly-initialized model of same architecture; a co-occurrence baseline (embeddings from training-corpus co-occurrence statistics / PPMI) to test whether the model exceeds surface co-occurrence structure; shuffled-label null for probes. 6. Generalization validation: for the periodic table, mask a subset of elements during property probing and test whether elements whose embeddings sit at the correct lattice position yield better held-out property extrapolation (e.g., electronegativity, atomic radius) than a co-occurrence baseline; for hierarchical ontologies, test held-out-entity property prediction using structural position. Correlate per-ontology RFS with generalization accuracy across models/sizes. 7. Scaling analysis: track RFS across model sizes to test whether ontology geometry emerges with scale. 8. Metrics: axis-recovery R^2, periodicity autocorrelation, cluster purity/silhouette, distance/cophenetic correlation, RFS, and RFS-vs-generalization Spearman/AUROC. Deliverable: an open per-ontology Relational-Geometry benchmark and leaderboard across public scientific models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Extracting clean per-entity embeddings is tokenization-dependent (elements may be multi-token, molecules vary in length); we standardize with minimal probe contexts and pooled representations, and report sensitivity to extraction choices. 2. A model may recover geometry simply because the training corpus co-occurrence already encodes it; the co-occurrence/PPMI baseline is central to distinguishing learned structure from surface statistics, and exceeding it is the key claim. 3. Geometry may be nonlinearly embedded; we use nonlinear dimensionality reduction (UMAP/kernel alignment) as robustness checks alongside linear axis recovery. 4. Ground-truth ontologies are cleaner in chemistry/materials than in biology (phylogenies are uncertain), so some ontologies support only qualitative or metric-correlation tests. 5. The generalization link is correlational; we report it as validation evidence and complement with per-ontology qualitative visualizations. 6. Availability and comparability of open models differ by domain, possibly restricting cross-model claims to within-domain comparisons, which is itself an informative scoping result.
